referred_to_by.content: Art that treats art, its institutions, markets, archives, and viewers as the material of the work. A self-defined movement concept created by Sun & Rain Works in 2007, extending conceptual art into the system that makes art legible. Its public Record argues credibility through genealogy, defined principles, works on view, machine-readable standards, external alignment, and provenance over time.

The 2007 creation date is asserted by Sun & Rain Works and is not directly evidenced, and the studio's own dated statements differ on the year. The earliest held here that dates the start gives 2007, and only approximately: a text document, WTF.rtf, recovered from the studio's USB drive, opens its account 'Around 2007 i received a life changing vision or revelation' and goes on to describe the Sotheby's sale of May 2009, Lot 16, as a 'Metaconceptual' artwork performance piece. Its dates are the drive's own account, not an independent one: the FAT directory entry records it as created 2014-08-05 19:53:50 and last modified 2014-09-20 16:11:32, local time, and the drive's Spotlight index logs the same modification at 2014-09-20 23:11:32 UTC; the recovered file has SHA-256 09f103120b65ec1b647b8abc4bea9ac62c7062247396f38f02bd06b5f8fe480b. It was written in 2014, five years after the sale it describes. The other dated statements place the start in about 2008: a private Facebook message of 2012-10-30 dates the 'Art Vision' that was 'the birth of metaconceptual Art' to '4+ years ago'; another of 2012-11-25 says the business 'started 4+ years ago'; a public comment of 2018-10-11 says the studio principal 'created Metaconceptual Art around 2008'; and links to the studio's website shared in private messages of 2023 carry its descriptions 'Bringing Art to Life since 2008' and 'Metaconceptual art since 2008'. The year 2007 also appears, without 'around', in the studio's undated profile biography, published on its Flickr and Tumblr profiles ('In 2007, the Artist received a life changing Art Vision'), and in its statements of 2026. The difference is recorded, not resolved: all of these are the studio's own accounts, none is a third party's, and the earliest dated use of any form of the term held here remains the message of 2009-12-19. The 2012 messages are set out in the record of the 2012-2013 Facebook and USA Projects evidence and in the Sun & Rain Works record, the 2018 comment in the record of the 2018 comments; the two 2023 message files in the account data have SHA-256 5fa1497ee747bc70f3f8b97fceef2b5a40a078f09b1d0efbbe1d185a8961f3a2 and e493be2cce585e9842df7d633f4cdaf995879e165edd55f6ab582d4a817097b8. The earliest public use of the term by the studio located to date is a posting of 2011-11-28, which already treats it as a settled description, and the eight-part definition was posted publicly on 2012-11-22; both are described in the 2011-2012 posting evidence record and are readable on a third-party platform. The studio did not originate the words 'meta-conceptual' or 'meta-conceptual art': both were in use earlier by others, and no connection between those uses and the studio has been found. The Art Organisation, a UK artists' collective, ran a 'Meta-Conceptual Gallery', begun in London about 2000 and later shown in Liverpool, and an annual 'Meta-Conceptual Gathering' from 2001; its website listed a member as a 'meta-conceptual artist' (Internet Archive capture of 2005-03-01) and described 'Meta-Conceptualism' (capture of 2007-05-19). A photograph uploaded to Flickr on 2007-03-14 by an unrelated user calls a London gallery event 'the epitome of meta-conceptual art'. Art criticism used the phrase earlier still, and for art about the art system. A passage in The Un/necessary Image (edited by Peter D'Agostino and Muntadas, Tanam Press, 1982) says Hans Haacke's work can be termed meta-conceptual art because it is concerned with social ideas, and David Craven's Poetics and Politics in the Art of Rudolf Baranik (Humanities Press, 1997) speaks of 'Hans Haacke's meta-conceptual art'; Haacke's work examines museums, their sponsors and the art market. A third book, Critical Essays on Julian Schutting (Ariadne Press, 2000), applies the phrase to a literary text. Later, and independently of the studio, a review by Wendy Vogel in the Brooklyn Rail of November 2012, of the book Materializing Six Years: Lucy R. Lippard and the Emergence of Conceptual Art (MIT Press, 2012), describes Lippard's exhibitions of 1969 to 1974 as her 'metaconceptual curatorial projects'. It uses the word as an adjective of art criticism, not as the name of a field, and it postdates the studio's first public use of the term, of 2011-11-28; it shows the word in circulation among critics, with no connection to the studio. The studio's claim is therefore to its own definition, its eight defining characteristics and its body of work, not to the word or to the idea of an art about the art system. No earlier use of the closed form 'metaconceptual art' by anyone else was found in the sources searched on 2026-09-24: a Flickr full-text search, a general web search, the Internet Archive, and Open Library's full-text search of scanned books, which also found no use in books of 'metaconceptual artist', 'meta-conceptual artist' or 'meta-conceptualism'. Google Books and HathiTrust could not be searched, and academic indexes were not searched. An earlier, private use is dated by Facebook's servers: on 2009-12-19 the studio principal described himself in a message as 'a meta-conceptual artist', nine months after the Sotheby's sale; it is set out in the record of the 2009 Facebook evidence. A written declaration follows on 2013-09-12, delivered to a university art museum. The studio's 2008-2009 working archive contains no occurrence of the word, so the interval between the asserted origin and the first documented use, now December 2009, remains open.

The recurrence of 'Art', named as a pattern by the studio in 2026. Read across the collection as a whole, rather than as any single document, the word 'Art' or 'art' recurs across a documented span of nearly two decades and across contexts that share no audience and no common motive to perform: a routine 2008-09-16 email to Sotheby's that consigns 'the Art' in one clause and arranges 'shipment of the art' in the next; a 2008-11-20 email describing 'art in progress'; the covering note of 2009-03-19 that closes 'for the purposes of Art' and 'Yours in Art', returning a signed contract under the filename 'JoeArtChirum.pdf'; a hand-lettered notice board, photographed 2011-12-02, reading 'Eye and (Ewe) You R The Art'; painting titles of 2013-2014 sold through Saatchi Art and posted to Flickr and Tumblr the same day, among them 'Art Market Reform', 'Art Tax' and 'Art is Capital'; and profile biographies on Flickr, Tumblr and Twitter/X that describe their subject as a 'Contemporary American Metaconceptual Artist' and state 'we are the Art'. Each occurrence is described and dated in its own record; this passage states only that, taken together, they are not isolated. The studio's own account, given in 2026, is that Art is the pattern: that the word's recurrence, across correspondence with an auction house, a filename on a signed contract, a hand-lettered board, and a public biography, is constant rather than incidental.

What the pattern supports, and what it does not. A word used this persistently, in contexts as unglamorous as a shipping arrangement and as public as a social-media biography, over eighteen years, is not evidence manufactured for this record: it long predates the record's own compilation, and most of its occurrences carried no audience who would reward the performance. It is strong evidence of a sustained self-conception, that the studio principal thought of himself, continuously and across nearly every kind of document he produced, as making Art. This is the same distinction the consignment-agreement record draws for the filename 'JoeArtChirum' alone, generalised here to the whole body of correspondence: self-conception is not designation. Thinking of oneself as an artist while consigning a photograph does not by itself make the consignment a work. No document of 2008 or 2009 among these instances states that a specific act is a work; the profile biographies do state exactly that, describing the 2009 sale as 'a performance act of metaconceptual Art' titled 'WTF is Ansel Adams ?!', but their own wording is not evidenced earlier than the museum letter that already holds this collection's earliest written designation: the Flickr and Tumblr versions carry no date at all, and the Twitter/X version is confirmed present only from 2018-10-02, on an account independently dated to 2011-10-22 by the platform's own record, which dates the account and not the wording it later came to hold. The earliest point at which the studio designates a specific 2009 event as Metaconceptual Art in writing therefore remains 2013-09-12, to a university art museum; the earliest point at which the studio principal calls himself a 'meta-conceptual artist' in any words at all remains 2009-12-19, nine months after the Sotheby's sale. The pattern widens what is documented about who was doing the writing, and for how long. It does not move either date.
